title: Internal Gear Pump

introduction.definition: An internal gear pump has a large outer rotor with internal teeth driving a smaller idler gear on an offset pin; a crescent-shaped partition separates the suction and discharge sides. Liquid fills the spaces between teeth as they unmesh, is carried around both sides of the crescent and is forced out as the teeth re-mesh.
applications: Viscous liquids: asphalt, molasses, resins, chocolate, adhesives
key_points: Excellent for high viscosity at low speed
introduction.summary: An internal gear pump has two gears of different sizes: an outer rotor with internal teeth, driven by the shaft, and a smaller idler with external teeth that runs on a fixed pin set off-centre. A crescent-shaped partition fills the space between them on the side away from the mesh. As the gears turn, teeth separate at the inlet and draw liquid in; it is carried around in pockets above and below the crescent and squeezed out as the teeth re-mesh at the outlet. Low shear, low speed and good suction make it ideal for viscous liquids.

parts.name: Casing (Pump Body)

parts.material: Cast iron, ductile iron, steel, stainless.

parts.name: Rotor (Internal Gear) & Shaft
parts.function: Driven internal gear that drives the idler and carries liquid in its tooth spaces.

parts.name: Idler Gear & Bushing
parts.function: External gear driven by the rotor; forms the inner pumping pockets.

parts.name: Head (Front Cover)
parts.function: Front cover carrying the idler pin and crescent; removable for service.

parts.name: Crescent & Idler Pin (on Head)
parts.function: Seals between rotor tooth tips and idler tooth tips to separate suction from discharge.

parts.function: Seals the rotating shaft where it leaves the pressurised casing.

piping: Size the suction line for low velocity (viscous liquids need large suction pipes); provide a strainer.
Fit a pressure-relief valve (integral or in the discharge line) — a positive-displacement pump will build pressure until something breaks if the discharge is blocked.
Support piping independently of the pump.
commissioning: Never start against a closed discharge valve.
Fill the pump with liquid (or ensure the suction is flooded) before start — avoid dry running unless the design allows it.
Heat jacketed pumps before start for viscous products.

periodic.task: Adjust end clearance as wear progresses.

video_tutorials.title: Internal Gear Pump — Introduction

script.narration: This module introduces the Internal Gear Pump.
An internal gear pump has a large outer rotor with internal teeth driving a smaller idler gear on an offset pin; a crescent-shaped partition separates the suction and discharge sides.
Liquid fills the spaces between teeth as they unmesh, is carried around both sides of the crescent and is forced out as the teeth re-mesh.
Typical applications include viscous liquids: asphalt, molasses, resins, chocolate, adhesives; fuel oil and lube oil; paints and inks; chemical transfer.
The cutaway reveals the internal construction: Casing (Pump Body), Rotor (Internal Gear) & Shaft, Idler Gear & Bushing, Head (Front Cover).
The exploded view separates every component so each one can be tapped for its function, material and failure modes.
Next, watch the operation tutorial to see how it works.

script.narration: How the Internal Gear Pump works.
Rotor and idler teeth unmesh at the suction port, creating expanding cavities.
Liquid is carried in the rotor teeth over the crescent and in the idler teeth under it.
Teeth re-mesh at the discharge port and push the liquid out.
The head carries the idler pin and crescent; end clearance is set at the head.
The flow overlay traces the liquid from suction to discharge.

video_tutorials.title: Internal Gear Pump — Maintenance

script.narration: Maintenance essentials for the Internal Gear Pump.
Check seal and noise.
Adjust end clearance as wear progresses.
Replace idler bushing and pin.
Watch for idler bushing wear: noise, flow loss. Common cause: poor lubricity, abrasives.
Watch for cavitation: noise. Common cause: speed too high for viscosity.
Record every inspection so trends — vibration, temperature, leakage and performance — can be compared over time.
